vendors.detail: Nearly every AI product in this directory was trained on NVIDIA silicon. On top of the chips sits a healthcare stack most clinicians never see: MONAI (the open-source standard for medical imaging AI), Parabricks (genomics acceleration), BioNeMo (biology foundation models), and partnerships from GE HealthCare to Mayo Clinic. NVIDIA takes a percentage of healthcare AI the way Levi Strauss took a percentage of the gold rush.
vendors.watch: GPU cost is becoming a healthcare cost. Every ambient scribe subscription and imaging AI license carries NVIDIA margin inside it.

vendors.name: Salesforce Health Cloud
vendors.desc: CRM logic applied to patients: Health Cloud runs member engagement, care coordination, and call centers for payers and systems that treat patients as customers.
vendors.detail: Health Cloud (2016) put patient relationships in the same machinery Salesforce built for sales pipelines: profiles, journeys, next-best-action. Payers and large systems use it for member services, referral management, and the front-door experience the EHR was never designed to handle. Agentforce brought agentic AI to those workflows. It lives in the gap between "patient" and "customer," which is exactly why clinicians tend to distrust it and administrators tend to buy it.
vendors.watch: Whether agentic AI in member services actually resolves problems or just deflects calls. The metric that matters is resolution, not containment.

vendors.name: Palantir
vendors.desc: Foundry as hospital operating picture: throughput, staffing, and capacity command centers at systems like Tampa General and Cleveland Clinic, plus the NHS Federated Data Platform.
vendors.detail: Palantir sells hospitals the thing it sold defense and intelligence: one operational picture over messy data. Bed capacity, OR schedules, discharge barriers, staffing, all in Foundry. Tampa General and Cleveland Clinic are flagship US deployments; the NHS England Federated Data Platform contract (2023, over 300M pounds) is the biggest and most contested example, with privacy groups fighting it from day one. A defense-adjacent data company inside public health infrastructure is a live policy question, not a settled one.
stats: Tampa General, Cleveland Clinic, HCA work
vendors.watch: The NHS deal is the test case. If it survives its critics and delivers, hospital command centers become a real Palantir market. If it collapses, healthcare stays a footnote for them.

vendors.name: UnitedHealth Group
vendors.desc: The largest healthcare company on earth: UnitedHealthcare insurance plus Optum, which employs or affiliates tens of thousands of physicians, runs a top PBM, and processes claims for its competitors.
vendors.detail: Around $400B in revenue. UnitedHealthcare covers roughly 50 million people, and Optum is the part most people underestimate: Optum Health (care delivery, one of the largest physician employers in America), Optum Rx (PBM), Optum Insight (the data and RCM engine that includes Change Healthcare, whose 2024 ransomware took down claims for the whole industry). Vertical integration this complete means UHG is frequently on both sides of the transaction. The DOJ has noticed. So has everyone who bills them.
vendors.watch: DOJ antitrust attention, Medicare Advantage billing scrutiny, and a leadership reset (Hemsley back as CEO in 2025). The integration that built the empire is now the thing regulators are circling.

vendors.name: CVS Health
vendors.desc: Pharmacy chain, largest PBM (Caremark), major insurer (Aetna), and primary care (Oak Street) in one company. The most complete payer-pharmacy-provider stack in retail reach.
vendors.detail: CVS assembled what Walmart and Walgreens tried and failed to build: ~$370B revenue across retail pharmacy, Caremark (the largest PBM by claims), Aetna (~27M medical members), and care delivery through Oak Street Health and Signify Health. The bet is that owning the pharmacy counter, the benefit design, and the clinic visit lets you manage cost end to end. The risk is that owning all three means answering for all three: PBM pricing practices are under sustained federal and state fire.
vendors.watch: PBM reform. If Congress or the FTC forces rebate and spread-pricing changes, the Caremark engine that funds the rest of the machine changes with it.

vendors.name: Cigna (Evernorth)
vendors.desc: A commercial insurer wrapped around Evernorth, home of Express Scripts, one of the big-three PBMs. Sold its Medicare Advantage business to focus on employers and pharmacy services.
vendors.detail: Cigna runs leaner than UHG or CVS on care delivery but holds the third seat in the PBM oligopoly through Express Scripts. The 2025 sale of its Medicare Advantage business to HCSC was a tell: Cigna is betting on employer-sponsored coverage and Evernorth services, and walking away from government programs. Roughly $247B in revenue, most of it flowing through pharmacy services, which surprises people who still think of Cigna as an insurance card.
vendors.watch: Same PBM reform exposure as CVS. Watch also whether stepping out of Medicare Advantage looks smart or early as MA economics keep deteriorating.

vendors.name: Elevance Health
vendors.desc: The Blue Cross giant (formerly Anthem): ~46M members across 14 Blue-branded state plans, building its own Optum-style services arm called Carelon.
vendors.detail: Elevance is what happens when a Blues plan decides to become a platform. Renamed from Anthem in 2022, it covers around 46 million people and is deliberately copying the UHG playbook: Carelon bundles the PBM (CarelonRx), behavioral health, and care services into a growth engine that sells beyond its own members. The Blues brand still carries local trust that national carriers envy, which is exactly the asset Elevance is using.
vendors.watch: Whether Carelon can become a real Optum competitor or stays a captive vendor. The gap between those two outcomes is enormous.

vendors.name: Humana
vendors.desc: The most Medicare-concentrated major payer: ~5.8M Medicare Advantage members plus CenterWell, its fast-growing senior primary care and home health arm.
vendors.detail: Humana went all-in on seniors: it exited employer group insurance entirely in 2023 to concentrate on Medicare Advantage and CenterWell (primary care clinics, home health, pharmacy built for the MA population). That focus made it the purest bet on MA economics among the majors, which was great until CMS star ratings slipped and reimbursement tightened. When MA sneezes, Humana catches pneumonia. Watch it as the leading indicator for the whole MA market.
vendors.watch: Star ratings recovery and MA rate cycles. Humana is the canary for whether Medicare Advantage stays the growth story the industry planned around.

vendors.name: Centene
vendors.desc: The largest Medicaid managed care company and the largest ACA marketplace insurer. The payer most exposed to public program policy, in both directions.
vendors.detail: Centene built a giant on the coverage programs other insurers treated as afterthoughts: Medicaid managed care contracts across dozens of states and the biggest ACA marketplace book in the country. That makes it less a market story than a policy story. Medicaid redeterminations, marketplace subsidy fights, state contract rebids: every one of them moves Centene more than any product launch. Its 2025 guidance shock over marketplace risk adjustment showed how fast policy exposure becomes financial exposure.
vendors.watch: The enhanced ACA subsidy fight and Medicaid funding changes land on Centene first. If you want to know what coverage policy is doing to real people, watch Centene enrollment numbers.

vendors.name: Oscar Health
vendors.desc: The insurtech that survived: tech-first ACA marketplace insurer that reached profitability in 2024 after a decade of losses, while its cohort (Bright, Friday, Clover pivots) collapsed around it.
vendors.detail: Oscar was supposed to prove software could reinvent insurance. What it actually proved is narrower and more interesting: a tech stack (member app, virtual care, its +Oscar platform) can make marketplace insurance operable at scale, but the economics are still insurance economics. First full-year profit in 2024, roughly 1.5 to 2 million members, almost all ACA marketplace. That concentration is its whole risk profile: subsidy policy IS the business model.
vendors.watch: The enhanced-subsidy fight in Congress. If subsidies shrink, marketplace enrollment shrinks, and Oscar has no second business to fall back on.

vendors.name: McKesson
vendors.desc: One of the three distributors that move nearly all US pharmaceuticals. ~$359B in revenue, top-ten on the Fortune 500, and the owner of CoverMyMeds.
vendors.detail: Founded in 1833 and still mostly invisible to patients: McKesson delivers roughly a third of all pharmaceuticals in North America, every day, on trucks nobody thinks about until they stop. It also owns CoverMyMeds (prior auth) and a large oncology practice network. Distribution margins are razor thin, which is why the big three (McKesson, Cencora, Cardinal) run on scale and logistics discipline that rivals any company on earth. The opioid settlements (about $7.4B over 18 years for McKesson) are the permanent asterisk on the record.
vendors.watch: Drug pricing policy and pharmacy economics. Distributors sit on the flow, so anything that changes the flow (tariffs, reform, shortages) hits them at once.

vendors.name: Cencora
vendors.desc: The second leg of the drug distribution oligopoly, formerly AmerisourceBergen. ~$300B in revenue with deep positions in specialty and biopharma services.
vendors.detail: Renamed from AmerisourceBergen in 2023, Cencora is the distributor with the strongest specialty pharmacy tilt: oncology drugs, cell and gene therapies, the high-cost products where handling and data matter as much as trucks. It also owns World Courier for clinical trial logistics. Walgreens held a major stake for years and has been selling it down. Same oligopoly math as McKesson: three companies, nearly the whole drug supply, margins under 1%.
vendors.watch: Specialty drug growth is the margin story. As more of drug spend becomes $100K+ therapies, the distributor that handles them best wins the decade.

vendors.name: Cardinal Health
vendors.desc: The third major distributor, and the one with a large medical-surgical products business alongside pharma: gloves, gowns, kits, and the supply closet of American hospitals.
vendors.detail: Cardinal moves drugs like McKesson and Cencora, but its distinguishing limb is medical products: a huge med-surg distribution and private-label manufacturing arm that stocks hospital supply rooms. That business showed its importance the hard way in 2020 when the PPE supply chain snapped. Cardinal has spent recent years restructuring it while the pharma segment keeps the lights on. Also runs at-home solutions and OptiFreight logistics.
vendors.watch: Med-surg turnaround and supply chain resilience policy. If Washington gets serious about onshoring medical supplies, Cardinal is at the center of it.

vendors.name: Medline Industries
vendors.desc: The largest private medical supplies manufacturer and distributor: ~$25B revenue, family-built, bought by Blackstone, Carlyle, and H&F in one of the largest PE healthcare deals ever (~$34B, 2021).
vendors.detail: Medline makes and distributes the unglamorous everything of care: exam gloves, drapes, skin prep, bed pads, surgical trays, over 335,000 products. It grew for decades as a family company out of Chicago before the 2021 buyout put it in private equity hands at a ~$34B valuation. An IPO has been in the works and repeatedly delayed by market conditions. Medline is the answer to a question clinicians rarely ask: who actually makes all this stuff?
vendors.watch: The IPO timing, and what PE ownership does to pricing on commodity supplies every hospital buys. Supply cost inflation is a quiet driver of hospital margins.

vendors.name: Owens & Minor
vendors.desc: A 140-year-old med-surg distributor trying to reinvent itself around home-based care, with a rocky recent run: its $1.36B Rotech acquisition was called off in 2025.
vendors.detail: Owens & Minor has distributed medical supplies since 1882 and owns Apria (home medical equipment) and Byram (home diabetes and wound supplies), the businesses it sees as its future. The plan to double down with Rotech fell apart in mid-2025 under regulatory delay, costing an $80M termination fee, and the company has been weighing the sale of its legacy products division. A case study in how hard it is to pivot a low-margin distribution giant while running it.
vendors.watch: Whether the home-based care pivot completes or stalls. Care is moving home; the question is whether a legacy distributor can follow it profitably.

vendors.name: GHX (Global Healthcare Exchange)
vendors.desc: The B2B ordering backbone of hospital supply chains: an exchange connecting thousands of provider organizations and suppliers, processing hundreds of billions in orders.
vendors.detail: GHX is what happens when an industry builds its own plumbing: founded in 2000 by a consortium of manufacturers to standardize hospital ordering, it became the dominant exchange where purchase orders, invoices, and item data flow between providers and suppliers. Nobody outside supply chain knows its name; nearly every hospital order touches it. Temasek took majority ownership from Thoma Bravo in 2021. The unglamorous moat: switching costs on infrastructure everyone shares.
vendors.watch: Supply chain data is becoming strategy: item-level cost and usage analytics are the upsell, and whoever owns the exchange owns the dataset.

vendors.name: Premier Inc
vendors.desc: One of the two giant group purchasing organizations: thousands of member hospitals aggregate buying power through Premier contracts, wrapped in a data and consulting arm.
vendors.detail: GPOs are the negotiators of American healthcare: Premier pools purchasing for roughly 4,350 hospitals and hundreds of thousands of other provider sites, taking administrative fees from suppliers in exchange for contract access. On top sits PINC AI, its data and analytics business built from decades of member cost and quality data. The GPO model itself is a standing policy argument (do fees distort supply markets?), which is why Premier shows up in Senate hearings as often as trade shows.
vendors.watch: GPO fee scrutiny and member consolidation. As health systems merge, they need Premier less; as costs rise, they need it more. Both are happening at once.

vendors.name: Vizient
vendors.desc: The largest GPO by purchasing volume (~$140B) and a major analytics and consulting force, formed from the merger of VHA, UHC, and Novation. Acquired Kaufman Hall in 2024.
vendors.detail: Vizient is the bigger, quieter twin of Premier: member-owned where Premier trades publicly, with around $140B in annual purchasing volume flowing through its contracts and the deepest clinical operations benchmark data in the industry (its academic medical center rankings move CEO bonuses). The 2024 Kaufman Hall acquisition added the consulting firm hospital boards call when the margins go red. If Premier is the public face of GPOs, Vizient is the establishment.
vendors.watch: The analytics arms race with Premier. Purchasing is the legacy business; the benchmark data on how hospitals actually perform is the strategic asset.

vendors.name: AMN Healthcare
vendors.desc: The largest public healthcare staffing company, riding the full whiplash of the travel nurse era: $5.2B revenue at the 2022 peak, roughly half that after rates normalized.
vendors.detail: AMN is the market bellwether for clinical labor. Travel nursing (Nursefinders roots, 1985), locum tenens, allied health, interim leadership, plus the tech layer: vendor management systems and its ShiftWise and language services lines. The COVID surge made travel staffing a $5B+ business for AMN; the correction cut revenue nearly in half and the stock further. What remains is the structural question: hospitals swear they will never depend on agency labor again, and they say it while posting agency requisitions.
vendors.watch: The permanent size of the contingent clinical workforce. If flexible staffing settles at 2-3x pre-COVID levels, AMN rebuilds; if hospitals actually insource, it shrinks for years.

vendors.name: Aya Healthcare
vendors.desc: The largest healthcare staffing firm in the country, private and platform-first. Walked away from its $615M acquisition of Cross Country in late 2025 under FTC pressure.
vendors.detail: Aya out-executed the incumbents on software: a marketplace where travel nurses see real jobs and real pay, layered over the old agency model. It passed AMN to become the biggest staffing firm in the country at the COVID peak. The attempted Cross Country acquisition would have consolidated the industry's top tier; faced with the FTC review, Aya terminated it in December 2025 and paid the $20M breakup fee. Still private, still founder-led, still the platform the others are measured against.
vendors.watch: Antitrust just redrew the map: if the big platforms cannot buy each other, they have to compete. Good news for nurses' pay transparency, hard news for margins.

vendors.name: CHG Healthcare
vendors.desc: The locum tenens pioneer and market leader, run from Utah: CompHealth, Weatherby Healthcare, and Global Medical Staffing place tens of thousands of physicians a year.
vendors.detail: CHG invented the modern locum tenens industry when CompHealth started covering rural Utah physician gaps in 1979, and it still leads it. Weatherby and CompHealth are the brands doctors know; the machine behind them runs from Midvale, Utah with a famously strong internal culture. Locums is the part of staffing that kept growing after the travel nurse correction, because physician shortages do not correct: they compound. One in four US physicians will work a locums assignment at some point.
vendors.watch: Physician shortage projections keep rising and rural coverage keeps thinning. Locums is becoming less of a stopgap and more of a delivery model, and CHG owns that shift.

vendors.name: Cross Country Healthcare
vendors.desc: The staffing firm left at the altar: Aya's $615M acquisition died in December 2025 under FTC review, leaving Cross Country independent in a consolidating market.
vendors.detail: Cross Country has done travel nursing, allied health, and workforce solutions since 1986 and rode the same boom-bust as everyone else. The Aya deal was its exit; twelve months of regulatory limbo killed it, and the $20M termination fee is thin consolation for a year of strategic paralysis. Now it faces the harder path: competing against bigger platforms (Aya, AMN) with a bruised stock and a workforce tech story (Intellify VMS) that has to carry more weight than before.
vendors.watch: Whether it finds another buyer the FTC will accept, retools as a tech-led VMS company, or gets slowly squeezed. The next 18 months decide which.

vendors.name: symplr
vendors.desc: The PE-assembled operations software roll-up: credentialing, provider data, workforce management, and compliance tools that most hospitals run somewhere in the back office.
vendors.detail: symplr is what happens when private equity applies the roll-up playbook to hospital operations software: dozens of acquisitions (API Healthcare for workforce management, Cactus and IntelliSoft for credentialing, Midas for quality) stitched into one vendor with enormous install-base reach and a mixed reputation for product velocity. Credentialing and provider data management sound boring until a physician cannot start seeing patients for 90 days because the paperwork engine is the bottleneck. That engine, at scale, is symplr.
vendors.watch: Credentialing delay is a real access-to-care problem. Watch whether symplr modernizes the stack or a startup unbundles it: 90-day onboarding is a target on someone's slide deck right now.

vendors.name: QGenda
vendors.desc: The dominant physician scheduling platform, now inside Hearst Health: who is on call, in which unit, at 3am, across 4,000+ organizations.
vendors.detail: QGenda solved a problem every hospital has and no EHR solved well: equitable, rules-based scheduling for physicians and increasingly for nurses and the whole clinical workforce. Call rules, credential windows, time-off equity, room assignments. Hearst Health (which also owns FDB and Zynx) acquired it in 2024, betting that workforce data belongs next to drug and clinical content data. Schedule data is quietly powerful: it knows about burnout before the surveys do.
vendors.watch: Scheduling data as a burnout and retention signal. The vendor that connects schedule equity to turnover prediction will get every CNO's attention.

vendors.name: ShiftKey
vendors.desc: The gig-economy model applied to nursing: a marketplace where licensed professionals (heavily CNAs and LPNs) bid on per-diem shifts at long-term care facilities as independent contractors.
vendors.detail: ShiftKey is the sharpest version of a controversial idea: clinicians as 1099 contractors bidding on individual shifts, mostly in nursing homes desperate for coverage. Facilities post shifts, professionals bid, software clears the market. Valued above $2B in 2023. The model fills real gaps in the most understaffed corner of healthcare, and it also imports every gig-economy fight (no benefits, classification lawsuits, race-to-the-bottom bid dynamics) into clinical care. Both things are true at once.
vendors.watch: Worker classification law. One adverse ruling on contractor status in a big state reshapes the whole gig-nursing model. Policy people are watching; so are plaintiffs' attorneys.

vendors.name: Vivian Health
vendors.desc: The transparency layer of healthcare staffing: a job marketplace (born NurseFly) where clinicians compare real pay across agencies, which disciplined the whole travel market.
vendors.detail: Vivian's core move was posting the number: actual weekly pay for travel contracts, side by side, across agencies. During the COVID pay spikes that transparency turned it into the Zillow of travel nursing and forced agencies to compete in the open. Incubated at IAC (which knows marketplaces), it aggregates permanent, travel, and per-diem listings with pay data as the draw. Its existence is why staffing agencies can no longer quote two nurses different rates for the same contract and hope they never compare notes.
vendors.watch: Transparency won; now the marketplace has to make money in a normalized rate environment. Watch the pivot from travel-boom traffic to durable perm-hiring revenue.

vendors.name: Amazon Health
vendors.desc: The most persistent big-retail push into care: One Medical primary care ($3.9B), Amazon Pharmacy with RxPass, after burying Haven and Amazon Care along the way.
vendors.detail: Amazon's healthcare history is a graveyard with a garden growing on it. Haven (the Buffett-Dimon-Bezos venture) died in 2021; Amazon Care died in 2022. What survived is more focused: One Medical (membership primary care, acquired 2023 for $3.9B, now bundled into Prime), Amazon Pharmacy (built on PillPack) with $5/month RxPass generics, and same-day med delivery expanding city by city. Amazon does not need healthcare margins; it needs Prime to be indispensable, and healthcare is the stickiest thing it has ever attached.
vendors.watch: Pharmacy same-day delivery scale. If Amazon makes prescriptions arrive like everything else it sells, the corner drugstore's last structural advantage erodes fast.

vendors.name: Apple Health
vendors.desc: The largest health device deployment in history without ever selling to a hospital: Apple Watch arrhythmia and sleep apnea detection, FDA-authorized AirPods hearing aids, and Health Records on the phone.
vendors.detail: Apple turned consumer hardware into screening infrastructure: irregular rhythm notifications and ECG on the Watch, sleep apnea detection (2024), fall detection, and the AirPods Pro hearing aid feature (FDA-authorized 2024) that put hearing assistance in millions of pockets overnight. Health Records pulls FHIR data from thousands of health systems onto the phone. Apple's play is not care delivery; it is owning the personal health record and the sensor layer, then letting clinicians deal with the tsunami of consumer-generated data it creates.
vendors.watch: The clinical workflow problem Apple created and did not solve: who reviews a million watch alerts? The next move (rumored AI health coaching) doubles down on consumer, not clinic.

vendors.name: Walgreens Boots Alliance
vendors.desc: The cautionary giant of retail health: VillageMD's ~$9B bet soured, the stock collapsed, and Sycamore Partners took it private for $10B in August 2025, splitting it into five companies.
vendors.detail: Walgreens spent the 2020s buying its way into care delivery (VillageMD, Summit Health, CityMD: nearly $9B) on the thesis that pharmacies plus clinics equals the future. The clinics lost money, hundreds of stores closed, and a century-old public company ended up sold to private equity for roughly what it once paid for its clinic bet alone. Sycamore closed the take-private in August 2025 and split the empire five ways: US retail, Boots, Shields, CareCentrix, and VillageMD, each standing alone. Pharmacy access in underserved neighborhoods now depends on PE portfolio math.
vendors.watch: Pharmacy deserts. PE owners close underperforming stores faster than public ones, and the neighborhoods losing their last pharmacy will be the ones that could least afford it.

vendors.name: Best Buy Health
vendors.desc: The retreat in progress: bought Current Health for $400M to power hospital-at-home, then sold it back to its founder in 2025 and pulled back to Lively senior devices.
vendors.detail: Best Buy's theory was elegant: Geek Squad installs technology in homes, so let it install care-at-home technology too. It bought GreatCall/Lively (2018, $800M) and Current Health (2021, $400M) and signed hospital-at-home partnerships. Then the economics arrived: a $109M restructuring, 161 layoffs, a $192M impairment, and in June 2025 Current Health was sold back to its co-founder for a fraction of the purchase price. What remains is the original, profitable idea: medical alert devices and senior connectivity. The lesson sits next to Walmart's: retail scale does not convert into care delivery.
vendors.watch: Whether ANY retailer besides pharmacy-anchored CVS makes care delivery work. The scoreboard so far reads: healthcare 3, retail 0.

vendors.name: Costco (Health)
vendors.desc: The anti-Walmart of retail health: no clinics, no acquisitions, just cheap known-price services bolted on quietly, including $29 telehealth visits through Sesame and famously low-margin pharmacy.
vendors.detail: While competitors bought clinic chains and wrote them down, Costco did what Costco does: member value with no drama. Pharmacy, optical, and hearing aids in-warehouse (its hearing aid prices are a running consumer-advocacy favorite), then a 2023 Sesame partnership adding $29 virtual primary care visits and discounted labs for members. No care-delivery risk on its books, no integration story to defend. It is a small bet, deliberately, and it is the only retail health strategy from the 2020s that has produced zero write-downs.
vendors.watch: Whether cash-price healthcare grows as deductibles climb. Costco members increasingly shop for care like they shop for tires, and Costco is positioned exactly there.

vendors.name: Kenvue
vendors.desc: The consumer health shelf in company form: Tylenol, Band-Aid, Listerine, Zyrtec, Neutrogena, spun out of J&J in 2023 and now being acquired by Kimberly-Clark for $48.7B.
vendors.detail: Kenvue is what Johnson & Johnson looked like to consumers, separated from the pharma company: the largest pure-play consumer health business on earth. Its short independent life has been eventful: activist investors, a politicized fight over unsupported Tylenol-autism claims from federal officials in 2025 that it had to publicly rebut with decades of evidence, and then the Kimberly-Clark acquisition (announced late 2025, shareholder-approved January 2026, closing expected late 2026). The OTC shelf is consolidating into ever-fewer corporate parents.
vendors.watch: What conglomerate ownership does to OTC brand trust, and whether evidence-free safety claims from officials keep forcing consumer health companies to run public science defenses.

vendors.name: Haleon
vendors.desc: The other consumer health spinoff: Sensodyne, Advil, Centrum, Voltaren, carved out of GSK and Pfizer's consumer businesses in 2022 as the world's largest standalone consumer health company by listing.
vendors.detail: Haleon was born from the same logic as Kenvue: pharma companies decided OTC brands deserve their own balance sheet. GSK and Pfizer pooled their consumer portfolios and listed it in London in 2022. Sensodyne and parodontax anchor an oral-health core that grows in every market; Advil and Voltaren carry pain relief; Centrum owns the vitamin aisle. Pfizer has been selling down its stake ever since. With Kenvue disappearing into Kimberly-Clark, Haleon becomes the last consumer-health pure play at global scale.
vendors.watch: Self-care economics: as out-of-pocket costs push patients toward the OTC aisle before the clinic, the companies that own that aisle end up with a bigger role in first-line care.

vendors.name: Procter & Gamble (Health)
vendors.desc: The healthcare business hiding inside a consumer goods giant: Vicks, Metamucil, Pepto-Bismol, Prilosec OTC, Align, and Oral-B add up to a ~$12B health segment most people never total up.
vendors.detail: P&G is a soap and diapers company by reputation and a top-tier consumer health company by the numbers: its Health Care segment (oral care plus personal health) runs around $12B a year, larger than most companies in this directory. Vicks alone is the first fever response in millions of households, which makes it de facto front-line healthcare. P&G will never call itself a healthcare company. That is precisely the point of including it: a real map of healthcare vendors includes the ones that reach patients before any clinician does.
stats: The medicine cabinet, not the clinic
vendors.watch: OTC as the pressure valve for an overloaded primary care system. When access tightens, self-care spending rises, and P&G measures that shift in scanner data before health policy sees it in claims.

vendors.name: Walmart Health
vendors.desc: The loudest retail health failure: 51 clinics and a telehealth arm, built on "everyday low prices" for care, all shut down in 2024 because the unit economics never worked.
vendors.detail: Walmart Health launched in 2019 with transparent cash prices ($40 checkups, $25 teeth cleanings) and a plan measured in hundreds of clinics. In April 2024 Walmart shut all 51 clinics and Walmart Health Virtual Care at once, saying plainly that reimbursement and operating costs made the business unsustainable. The retail giant that reshaped grocery pricing could not make primary care pencil out. Pharmacies and vision centers remain. The lesson the whole industry took: foot traffic does not equal care delivery, and low prices cannot fix underlying cost structure.
vendors.watch: Every future "retail will disrupt healthcare" pitch now has to explain why Walmart could not do it. That is the standard the next entrant has to clear.

vendors.name: Solventum
vendors.desc: The 3M healthcare business as a standalone company, and the quiet giant of medical coding: 360 Encompass and the grouper methodologies behind a huge share of US inpatient coding.
vendors.detail: When 3M spun off its healthcare division in April 2024, the HIM world paid closer attention than Wall Street did: Solventum inherited 360 Encompass, the computer-assisted coding and CDI platform embedded in thousands of hospitals, plus the APR-DRG methodology that payers and states use to classify inpatient stays. It also makes Tegaderm dressings, Littmann stethoscopes, and dental products, and sold its purification unit to Thermo Fisher for $4.1B. A generation of HIM coders grew up on "the 3M encoder." It has a new name now.
vendors.watch: AI-native coding startups are aiming directly at the encoder incumbency. Solventum has to modernize 360 Encompass faster than autonomous coding vendors erode it. That is the race.

vendors.name: Unite Us
vendors.desc: The referral rails for social care: closed-loop networks connecting health systems, payers, and community organizations for food, housing, and transportation needs.
vendors.detail: Founded by veterans who watched fellow veterans bounce between disconnected services, Unite Us builds the referral infrastructure between healthcare and social services: a clinician screens for food insecurity, sends a closed-loop referral to a food bank, and actually learns whether the family got fed. States and payers buy statewide networks of it. The hard part was never the software; it is sustaining community organizations' participation when their funding does not pay for data entry. SDOH tech rises and falls with policy attention to it.
vendors.watch: SDOH funding is policy-cyclical. When value-based care money tightens, social care screening is the first line item questioned, and the referral networks feel it immediately.

vendors.name: Findhelp
vendors.desc: The open search layer for social services, born as Aunt Bertha: the largest directory of food, housing, and assistance programs in the country, searchable by ZIP code by anyone.
vendors.detail: Findhelp took the opposite approach from Unite Us and built an open platform. Anyone can search findhelp.org by ZIP code and find food pantries, rent assistance, and utility programs; health systems and payers license the embedded version for their workflows. Founded in Austin in 2010 as Aunt Bertha, it built the underlying program directory that much of the SDOH ecosystem depends on. Open access versus closed-loop accountability is the structural argument of the whole social-care-tech space, and these two companies are its poles.
vendors.watch: Directory accuracy at scale is brutal: programs close, numbers change, eligibility shifts. The moat is maintenance, and maintenance is exactly what nobody funds.
